caveats: ERA5 is a ~31 km reanalysis, not station truth; grid-cell verification favours smooth models and understates local extremes.
ECMWF AIFS is trained on ERA5, so verification against ERA5 is expected to favour it; its advantage against station observations may be smaller.
Single grid points stand in for each region; production-weighted areal averages would score differently.
Previous-Runs data stitch successive runs issued N days earlier, so a "day-3" forecast mixes run times within the target day.

Diebold–Mariano tests use the case-weighted daily loss differential with a 14-day Newey–West bandwidth (robustness at the lead, 7 and 21 days reported); sites are not independent, so the effective sample is the number of days, and a handful of calendar days with no complete cases are skipped.

Raw-ensemble CRPS treats the m members (7 at day 1, 5–6 at longer leads) as an empirical distribution, which carries a finite-ensemble penalty; the zero-training Gaussian baseline and the fair CRPS isolate how much of the gain is learned from past errors.
Model membership per region and lead is fixed from availability over the whole archive (no truth or skill information is used).
An exploratory first run scored early methods over the whole period, including the confirmation days; only forecasts after 2026-11-16 are strictly unseen (--period prospective).

v3tests.description: Diebold–Mariano tests of Astraeus v3 against Astraeus v2 (case-weighted daily CRPS differential v3 − v2; negative = v3 better; Newey–West bandwidth 14 d with HLN correction; robustMaxP = largest p over bandwidths lead, 7, 14, 21 d). Produced after the freeze by re-running the frozen final suite with astraeus-v2 added to the comparison list of a temporary, uncommitted copy of research/weather-benchmark.ts; the confirmation run reproduced the published summary exactly. Not part of the pre-specified selection or adoption rules.

caveats: Coverage is uneven: Tmax at 7 of 16 sites and precipitation at 6, all but one in the United States, Australia and the Netherlands. The tropical and Southern-Hemisphere crop sites (Mato Grosso, Paraná, Minas Gerais, Daloa, Mekong) and Punjab, Beauce, Odesa and Jilin have no usable station, so station results describe mid-latitude, data-rich sites only.

GHCN-Daily records for the non-U.S. synoptic stations near these sites stop in August 2025; Meteostat fills its 2025–2026 daily files at the same stations with model forecasts (DWD MOSMIX, MET Norway), which are excluded here — verifying forecasts against model-filled “observations” would be circular.

Representativeness: a station is a point 4–12 km from the grid point the forecasts were fetched for; station-minus-grid differences (elevation, coast, urban heat) are part of the station error and are not forecastable by the raw models. Forecasts were not refetched at station coordinates (Open-Meteo budget).

Day conventions: forecasts and ERA5 are UTC days; station days are local (US ASOS midnight LST, Dubbo 9 am local for rainfall). The integer shift fixed on development data aligns the bulk of each day but cannot remove the 4–6-hour local-vs-UTC offset, which blurs precipitation more than Tmax.

Tmean is not verified on stations: (Tmax+Tmin)/2 differs systematically from the 24-hour mean the forecasts are aggregated to, and the forecast cache holds no daily minimum to build a like-for-like (max+min)/2.

Mode (b) trains on the same station it is verified on, with the same 6-day lag and windows as the ERA5-trained system; it is the realistic upper bound for site-specific calibration, not a deployable product for sites without a live station feed.
Climatology reference: the station’s own 2019–2024 record where ≥ 60% complete; Córdoba Tmax (Meteostat METAR-derived, 47% complete) uses the ERA5 grid-point climatology instead.

caveats: Confirmation period only (test days 2026-04-01 → 2026-11-08): area forecasts were fetched from 2025-12-15 to fit the Open-Meteo budget, which leaves no development-period history for the areas.

Climatology uses ERA5 2022–2024 for both the areas and the single points in this comparison (3 years to fit the budget; the published benchmark uses 2019–2024), so CRPSS vs climatology here is not comparable with the published table.
Four points per area: the area mean is a 4-point production-weighted average, not a full areal integral; it removes much but not all small-scale noise.

Skill differences compare scores on different truths (area-mean ERA5 vs grid-point ERA5): the area mean is smoother and easier to forecast, so CRPS levels fall; the question is whether post-processing gains (CRPSS) survive, not whether CRPS is lower.

Model membership is fixed per run from availability (≥ 90% of days) over each run’s own archive. UK Met Office day-1 forecasts have a gap of about six weeks in April–May 2026 in the Previous-Runs archive: over the single points’ full archive (from 2025-07-01) the model passes the rule, over the shorter area archive (from 2025-12-15) it does not, so day-1 area forecasts use 6 models and day-1 point forecasts 7. Leads 3–7 use identical models.
ERA5 remains the truth here; production-weighted station networks would be the natural next step.

caveats: The weather index is CPC CONUS degree days for truth, but forecasts come from nine city points mapped to CPC census-division averages; the representativeness oracle (2b) measures the loss from that mapping separately from forecast error.
The weather week (Central local days Friday–Thursday) leads the EIA storage week (09:00 CST Friday to Friday) by nine hours.

Forecasts use runs initialised no later than Thursday 23:00 CT (the Friday 00 UTC cycle at the latest) for the week whose first gas day starts Friday 09:00 CT; dissemination latency of that last cycle (~4–8 h) still precedes the week start.

The 2010–June 2015 storage history consists of EIA-derived estimates; reclassifications before November 2015 are not documented in revisions.xls and remain in the target. Multi-week restatements (2017, 2024, 2025–26) are adjusted only in their first week.
The EIA five-year average is recomputed from today’s revised history with EIA’s daily-interpolation method; EIA’s published values at release time used the history then available.
Weekly weather explains demand-side variation only; production, LNG feed-gas outages, pipeline maintenance and price-driven fuel switching are left to the seasonal/trend terms.
Previous Runs archives start in March 2021 (GFS) and February 2024 (ECMWF IFS), so the primary window is ~2.7 years; the longer GFS window is the better-powered test.

The missing GFS block (listed above) is the January–February 2024 period, which includes the record withdrawal of the January 2024 Arctic outbreak; such weeks are where the five-year average errs most, so their absence more likely understates than overstates the forecast’s skill, but it is untested.

Targets and training use today’s revised EIA history and CPC files (data vintage of the fetch date), not the values available in real time; two restatement steps (May 2024, Aug 2025) were inferred from original vs revised stocks.

The nine-city index reads warm against CPC in winter: the Dec–Feb weekly HDD bias is negative for ERA5 at the cities and for every forecast in the verification table. It therefore comes from the pooled-season city→CPC linear map, not from the forecasts. It works against the forecast model (fitted on CPC truth), so it can only reduce the reported skill; a season-specific map is an obvious improvement for a future version.
Open-Meteo free API: non-commercial research use only.
